questions.topic: Refraction angle from Snell's law
questions.learningObjective: apply Snell's law to find a refraction angle
questions.stem: Light passes from air, where its speed is 3.00e8 m/s, into glass of refractive index 1.50 at an incidence angle of 30.0 degrees to the normal. What is the refraction angle in the glass, in degrees?
questions.explanation: An index of 1.50 means the light slows to 2.00e8 m/s in the glass, and Snell's law in its speed form, the sine of the angle divided by the speed being equal on the two sides, gives the sine of the new angle as 2.00e8 times the sine of 30.0 degrees over 3.00e8 = 0.3333, whose arcsine is 19.47 degrees. Written with indices instead, 1.00 times the sine of 30.0 degrees over 1.50, the same 0.3333 comes out, because the index already is the ratio of the two speeds, and the two forms must agree. Dividing by 0.667 rather than by 1.50 applies that speed ratio a second time and gives 48.59 degrees, which is the characteristic way to get this wrong.
questions.hint: Write sin of the angle in air divided by the index equals the sine of the angle in the glass.

The boundary only does this when light is going from the denser medium to the rarer one, since otherwise no angle can ever push the refracted ray past 90 degrees. Angles larger than this one are the ones for which total internal reflection is possible.

Checking with the magnification, which is minus the image distance over the object distance = -0.500, confirms a real image at half the object's size, and a real image beyond a lens comes from an object beyond its focal point, which 0.600 m is. Subtracting the object term the other way round would give a negative distance and wrongly suggest a virtual image.
questions.hint: Rearrange the lens equation so the image distance stands alone, then check the sign.

questions.stem: A prism of apex angle 60.0 degrees has a refractive index of 1.50 for red light and 1.54 for violet light. What is the angular dispersion between those two colours, in degrees?

That gap exists only because the index is not the same for the two colours, the index rising as the wavelength falls, so violet is bent more than red. questions.learningObjective: compute a grating angle from line density and wavelength
questions.stem: A grating ruled with 400 lines per millimetre is used with light of wavelength 500 nm. What angle, in degrees, does the first-order maximum make with the grating's normal?

options.text: 11.5 degrees, since the sine of the angle is wavelength over spacing
5.7 degrees, which halves the angle because two orders are involved
options.misconception: divides the angle as though the second order were being sought

options.text: 23.1 degrees, which doubles the angle for the same first-order maximum
options.misconception: doubles the angle in place of doubling the order number

options.text: 0.20 degrees, which reads the sine value as though it were in degrees
options.misconception: reports the sine as though it were the angle itself

questions.explanation: Four hundred lines per millimetre is a spacing of 2.5e-6 m, and the first-order maximum needs a path difference of one wavelength across that spacing, so the sine of the angle is 500e-9 over 2.5e-6 = 0.200 and the angle is 11.54 degrees. Going to the second order would double that path difference and so raise the sine to 0.400, giving 23.6 degrees rather than doubling the first-order angle, which is why the angle does not scale linearly with the order. At 0.200 radians the small-angle approximation is still good, so a straight-line estimate happens to be close but not exact.
questions.hint: Convert the line density to a spacing, then take the arcsine of the wavelength over it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Spotting the impossible lens entry
questions.learningObjective: identify the lens reading that breaks the lens equation
questions.stem: A bench test of one converging lens lists object and image distances of 0.300 m giving 0.600 m, 0.400 m giving 0.400 m, and 0.200 m giving 0.200 m. Which entry cannot be correct?

options.text: The 0.200 m entry, since an object at the focus images at infinity
The 0.300 m entry, which should read 0.900 m for this lens
options.misconception: rejects the reading that fixes the focal length

options.text: The 0.400 m entry, which should read 0.800 m for this lens
options.misconception: rejects the case where object and image distances are equal

options.text: No entry is wrong, since each image distance falls as the object moves in
options.misconception: accepts a falling column without applying the lens equation

questions.explanation: The first two entries agree on one focal length, since 1 over 0.300 plus 1 over 0.600 and 1 over 0.400 plus 1 over 0.400 both come to 5.000 per metre, that is 0.200 m, and the third entry demands a focal length of 0.100 m instead, so the lens cannot be the same one. Physically an object exactly at the focal point sends all the refracted rays out parallel, so the image is at infinity and no finite image distance exists at all. A column that merely decreases is not evidence of consistency, since the lens equation constrains the reciprocals rather than the raw distances.
questions.hint: Find the focal length from the first two entries, then test the third against it.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Index read from a prism deviation log
questions.learningObjective: deduce a refractive index from a recorded prism deviation
questions.stem: A prism log records an apex angle of 60.0 degrees with minimum deviations of 30.0 degrees for red light and 32.4 degrees for violet light. What refractive index does that imply for violet?

options.text: 1.54, since the deviation is the index less one times the apex
1.50, which is the index the red deviation implies instead
options.misconception: reports the long-wavelength index for the short wavelength

options.text: 0.54, which is the deviation over the apex with the one left out
options.misconception: forgets to add one to the deviation-to-apex quotient

options.text: 1.08, which doubles the quotient instead of adding one to it
options.misconception: doubles the quotient rather than completing it

questions.explanation: At minimum deviation a prism's deviation equals the index less one times the apex angle, so the index is 1 + 32.4 over 60.0 = 1 + 0.540 = 1.540 for violet, while the red entry gives 1 + 30.0 over 60.0 = 1.500. The two indices differ by 0.040, and that difference is the whole of the prism's angular dispersion of 2.4 degrees when multiplied back by the apex angle. The added one is what makes the index dimensionless and greater than one, and leaving it out gives a number that is a pure angle fraction instead.
questions.hint: Divide the deviation by the apex angle and add one to the result.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Power of a pair of lenses in contact
questions.learningObjective: evaluate the combined power of two lenses in contact
questions.stem: A trial frame holds a lens of power +2.00 dioptres in contact with a lens of power -3.00 dioptres. What power does the pair present to the light, in dioptres?

options.text: -1.00 D, since the powers of lenses in contact add algebraically
-6.00 D, which multiplies the two powers instead of adding them
options.misconception: multiplies powers rather than summing them

options.text: +1.00 D, which adds the magnitudes and drops the weaker lens's sign
options.misconception: ignores the sign of the diverging lens's power

options.text: +5.00 D, which subtracts the smaller power from the larger one
options.misconception: subtracts the powers instead of adding them

questions.explanation: The power of a lens in dioptres is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, and lenses in contact add their powers, so +2.00 plus -3.00 = -1.00 D, equivalent to a diverging lens of focal length -1.00 m. The sign is decided by which lens has the larger power in magnitude, and here the diverging lens at 3 dioptres outweighs the converging one at 2, so the pair diverges. The result is what a spectacles prescription works in, since a prescription is simply a sum of lens powers intended to cancel the eye's own error.
questions.hint: Add the two powers with their signs, since a contact pair shares one surface spacing.

questions.topic: Smallest gap a telescope can resolve
questions.learningObjective: convert an angular resolution limit into a linear separation
questions.stem: An observer sights two points 1500 m away through a telescope of aperture 0.080 m at a wavelength of 550 nm. What is the smallest gap between those points, in mm, that the instrument can resolve?

options.text: 12.6 mm, which is the diffraction angle times the distance
10.3 mm, which omits the factor of 1.22 for a round aperture
options.misconception: drops the circular-aperture factor from the Rayleigh criterion

options.text: 25.2 mm, which doubles the angle as though two beams were involved
options.misconception: doubles the resolved angle instead of halving the gap

options.text: 0.080 mm, which uses the aperture as the smallest resolvable gap
options.misconception: treats the aperture size as a linear resolution

questions.explanation: The Rayleigh angle for that aperture is 1.22 times 550e-9 over 0.080 = 8.3875e-6 rad, and a gap of 1500 m subtends that angle when it equals 8.3875e-6 times 1500 = 0.01258 m, that is 12.6 mm. Leaving out the 1.22 gives 10.3 mm, which is the answer for a slit rather than a round aperture and is a genuine near miss. The conversion needs the distance as well as the angle, so an angular limit on its own never answers a question about a gap between two objects.
questions.hint: Find the Rayleigh angle first, then multiply by the distance to the objects.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Cladding index from a measured critical angle
questions.learningObjective: deduce a cladding index from a critical angle measurement
questions.stem: The core of an optical fibre has index 1.50 and a test measures its critical angle at the core-cladding boundary as 79.0 degrees. What index does the cladding have?

options.text: 1.47, which is the core index times that sine
1.53, which divides the core index by that sine instead
options.misconception: divides by the sine rather than multiplying by it

options.text: 1.50, which would follow if light met the boundary normally
options.misconception: assumes a cladding of equal index could still guide light

options.text: 1.06, which uses a 45 degree angle in place of the measured one
options.misconception: substitutes a guessed angle for the measured critical angle

questions.explanation: At the critical angle the sine of that angle is the cladding index over the core index, so the cladding index is 1.50 times the sine of 79.0 degrees = 1.50 times 0.98163 = 1.472, that is 1.47, just below the core as total internal reflection requires. The division in the second option would give 1.53, a value above the core, and light could not be trapped at all. A cladding index equal to the core's gives a critical angle of 90 degrees and no usable guidance either, since every ray would sit exactly at the limit rather than beyond it.
questions.hint: Multiply the core index by the sine of the measured critical angle.

questions.topic: Reading glasses for a near point
questions.learningObjective: compute the lens power that brings a page to a near point
questions.stem: A reader whose nearest clear vision is 20.0 cm wants to read a page held 25.0 cm away. What lens power, in dioptres, brings the page to their near point?

options.text: +1.00 D, since the power is one over 0.20 less one over 0.25
-1.00 D, since the correction must weaken the eye's own power
options.misconception: supposes a near-point correction must diverge the light

options.text: +4.00 D, which is one over the near point with the page ignored
options.misconception: ignores the working distance when forming the power

options.text: +5.00 D, which is one over the working distance with nothing subtracted
options.misconception: uses only the working distance as though it were the near point

questions.explanation: The correction must make an object at 25.0 cm look to the eye like an object at 20.0 cm, so the required power is 1 over 0.20 m less 1 over 0.25 m = 5.00 minus 4.00 = +1.00 D, a converging lens that does the focusing the ageing eye can no longer manage. The sign is positive because the eye needs more power for near work, not less, and this is the ordinary reading-glasses prescription for a presbyopic reader. Working in centimetres without converting would give a number a hundred times too large, which is the usual slip in this calculation.
questions.hint: The page must appear at the near point, so subtract the reciprocals of the two distances in metres.

questions.topic: Expression for linear magnification
questions.learningObjective: state the expression for linear magnification
questions.stem: Which expression gives the linear magnification produced by a lens or a mirror from the distances involved?

options.text: Minus the image distance over the object distance, from two similar triangles
Plus the image distance over the object distance, with the sign dropped
options.misconception: drops the minus sign that carries the image orientation

options.text: The object distance over the image distance, since the sizes swap that way
options.misconception: inverts the ratio of image size to object size

options.text: The focal length over the object distance, with no minus sign
options.misconception: uses a ratio that is not a magnification at all

questions.explanation: The lens or mirror and the two similar triangles formed by the ray through the centre give the ratio of image height to object height as the image distance over the object distance, and the leading minus sign records that a real image is inverted, since the two triangles lie on opposite sides of the axis. The formula is identical for a thin lens and a spherical mirror, since both are derived from the same small-angle geometry. The sign is the only part that is convention-dependent, and dropping it loses the orientation of every real image.
questions.hint: Compare the two similar triangles and remember that a real image is inverted.

questions.topic: Expression for double-slit fringe spacing
questions.learningObjective: state the expression for double-slit fringe spacing
questions.stem: Light of wavelength lambda passes a double slit of separation d onto a screen a distance L away. Which expression gives the fringe spacing for small angles?

options.text: lambda times L over d, which comes from the pattern's similar triangles
d times L over lambda, which puts the slit spacing on top
options.misconception: inverts the dependence on wavelength and slit separation

options.text: lambda times d over L, which inverts the dependence on distance
options.misconception: puts the screen distance in the denominator of the fringe spacing

options.text: The square root of lambda times L over d, as for a round aperture
options.misconception: borrows a square root from the resolution criterion

questions.explanation: Successive bright fringes are one wavelength apart in path difference, the small-angle geometry turns that into a screen separation of lambda L over d, and every term's dependence follows from there: a longer wavelength widens the pattern, a larger slit separation narrows it, and a further screen magnifies it. The same lambda over d appears as the sine of the fringe angle, so the spacing on the screen is that angle times the screen distance, and dropping the distance leaves an angle rather than a position. A square root belongs to the Rayleigh criterion for a circular aperture, not to the double-slit geometry.
questions.hint: Get the fringe angle as lambda over d, then multiply by the distance to the screen.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: A claim the lens equation contradicts
questions.learningObjective: explain why a fixed image distance cannot hold for every object distance
questions.stem: A designer claims that a converging lens of focal length 0.200 m will form its image 0.600 m behind the lens for every object placed anywhere in front of it. Use the lens equation to explain why that claim cannot be right.

answer.exemplar: The lens equation inverts to 1 over the image distance as 1 over 0.200 minus 1 over the object distance, so the image distance is explicitly a function of the object distance rather than a fixed property of the lens. Setting the image distance to 0.600 m forces 1 over the object distance to be 5.000 minus 1.667 = 3.333 per metre, that is an object distance of exactly 0.600 m, so the claim holds for one object position and no other. An object at 0.300 m gives 1 over the image distance as 5.000 - 3.333 = 1.667, an image at 0.600 m, an object at 0.400 m images at 0.400 m, and an object at 0.150 m, inside the focal point, gives a negative image distance, meaning a virtual image on the object's own side. The image distance is set by the pair of the lens focal length and the object distance together, so quoting one without the other cannot characterise the lens at all.

questions.explanation: A complete answer isolates the image distance in terms of the object distance, shows the object distance that would produce the claimed 0.600 m, gives at least one contrasting case, and notes that an object inside the focal length reverses the sign of the image distance.
questions.hint: Rearrange the lens equation so the object distance appears, and see what it must be.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Tracing why a diverging lens cannot make a real image
questions.learningObjective: explain by ray tracing why a diverging lens only forms virtual images
questions.stem: By tracing what the refracted rays from a real object actually do, explain why a diverging lens can only ever form a virtual image.

answer.exemplar: Take one ray from the tip of a real object parallel to the principal axis. A diverging lens refracts it so that it spreads as though it had come from the near focus, so the ray leaves travelling downwards and backwards along the line through that focus. Take a second ray aimed at the centre of the lens, which passes straight through without deviation because the two faces meet at that angle. Followed forwards, the two rays diverge and can never meet, and followed backwards, the first crosses the axis at the focus, so the only place they appear to meet is behind the lens. Any third ray behaves the same way, since the lens acts identically on every ray from the same object point, so the emerging bundle is always diverging and only its backward extensions converge. Because the rays that reach the eye are spreading out, the eye traces them backwards to an apparent image behind the lens, and by definition that image is virtual. The algebra agrees, since 1 over a negative focal length minus 1 over any positive object distance is always negative, so the image distance is negative at every object position.

questions.explanation: A full answer traces two rays from one object point, notes that they diverge and meet only on backward extension, identifies the result as a virtual image by definition, and can confirm it with the sign of the image distance from the lens equation.
questions.hint: Follow a ray parallel to the axis and one through the centre, then watch whether they meet.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a simple lens fringes white light
questions.learningObjective: explain the origin of chromatic aberration in a simple lens
questions.stem: Explain why white light passed through a simple single lens produces a blurred image fringed with colour rather than one uniformly sharp picture.

answer.exemplar: White light is a spread of wavelengths, and glass slows the short wavelengths more than the long ones, so its refractive index is largest for violet and smallest for red. A lens's focal length is fixed by that index, so violet focuses nearer the lens than red, and the gap between those two focal lengths is the chromatic aberration. Because each colour forms its own image of a different size, no single plane holds them all in focus at once: a point source is seen as a small spectrum, with violet on the side nearer the lens, and the blur grows with distance from the axis. The effect is present even in a single colour of light, which is what separates it from spherical aberration, and it is why camera objectives contain several elements of different types of glass chosen so that their dispersions partly cancel while their powers add. Stopping the aperture down reduces the coloured fringes but also dims the image, so it is a trade rather than a cure.

questions.explanation: A complete answer links the spread of wavelengths to a spread of refractive indices, connects the index spread to a spread of focal lengths, notes the resulting size difference between colour images, and identifies the cure as an achromatic combination of glasses.
questions.hint: The lens's focal length depends on the index, so ask what the index does across the colours.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Why a third polariser restores light
questions.learningObjective: explain how inserting a third polariser lets light past a crossed pair
questions.stem: Explain how two polarisers crossed at right angles can block light completely, yet a third polariser inserted between them at 45 degrees lets a quarter of the original intensity through.

answer.exemplar: The first ideal polariser transmits only the component of the unpolarised light along its own axis, so the light leaving it is completely polarised along that direction and half the original intensity. The second polariser's axis is at 90 degrees to that, so the arriving light has no component along it at all and the intensity emerging is zero; nothing is cancelled by interference, the component simply is not present. Insert a third polariser at 45 degrees to the first: the light leaving it is now polarised at 45 degrees, since a polariser imposes its own axis on whatever reaches it, and the second polariser is then only 45 degrees from that direction and transmits the cosine squared of 45 degrees, that is one half, of what reached it. Chained, that is one half of the half the first polariser passed, so a quarter of the original intensity emerges, from a pair that passed nothing. The lesson is that the rule transmits a fraction cosine squared of the angle between consecutive axes, and inserting an element changes the polarisation of the light that the next one sees.

questions.explanation: A full answer explains that the first polariser sets the polarisation along its axis, that the crossed second has nothing to transmit, and that the third re-imposes a 45 degree polarisation so the cosine squared rule passes half of what reached it.
questions.hint: Track the polarisation of the light arriving at each element, not just the angles of the axes.
